topic: U.S. consumer demand: nominal spending growth, uneven regional experience, and price pressure
audience_relevance: Korean-language readers comparing U.S. demand indicators need to distinguish dollar sales growth, price changes, and regional business anecdotes; this package makes no Korea trade or investment impact claim.
selected_reason: A current Fed regional report and contemporaneous federal retail-price releases allow a useful comparison of what each measure can and cannot establish.
cutoff_note: Checked on 2026-10-28. Fed contacts collected through Oct. 5; September CPI and retail sales; August BEA PCE. September BEA release scheduled for Oct. 29 and was not yet available at cutoff.

facts.fact: The October Beige Book said two of 12 Districts reported moderate economic growth; three modest, four slight, and three no significant change.
facts.evidence_location: National Summary > Overall Economic Activity; lines 7-8
facts.scope_note: Qualitative regional contacts; not a national household survey.

facts.fact: Most Districts reported little or no change in consumer spending; over half said spending was driven by high-income households.
facts.evidence_location: National Summary > Overall Economic Activity; line 8
facts.scope_note: Report of contacts, not measured household expenditure shares.

facts.fact: Beige Book information was collected on or before October 5, 2026; the report says it summarizes comments from outside the Federal Reserve and is not a commentary on officials' views.
September 2026 advance U.S. retail and food services sales were $745.0 billion, up 0.8% month over month and 6.3% year over year; the sales estimates are not adjusted for price changes.
facts.scope_note: Seasonally and calendar adjusted, but nominal/current-dollar sales.

facts.fact: September CPI-U increased 0.6% seasonally adjusted month over month and 3.7% over 12 months on an unadjusted basis; gasoline rose 9.1% in the month and accounted for over half of the monthly all-items increase.
facts.scope_note: Do not subtract from Census retail growth to infer real sales; baskets and methods differ.

facts.fact: The CPI index excluding food and energy rose 0.3% in September and 2.6% over the 12 months ending September.
facts.scope_note: Core CPI measure, not a forecast of future inflation.

facts.fact: August 2026 personal consumption expenditures in current dollars increased $190.8 billion, or 0.9%; the personal saving rate was 4.1%.
facts.scope_note: August, current-dollar estimate; not the same period or coverage as September retail sales.

facts.fact: BEA's page listed September 2026 Personal Income and Outlays as the next release on October 29, 2026.
facts.scope_note: As of the October 28 article cutoff, the September release had not yet occurred.

independent_source_note: The four sources are primary publications from three U.S. federal agencies. Census, BLS, and BEA statistics directly measure separate indicators; the Fed Beige Book is qualitative contact reporting. They are complementary, not independent replications of the same measure.
conflicts_or_limits: Nominal sales growth is not real volume growth.
CPI and retail trade have different baskets and methods; do not derive a real retail growth estimate by subtracting their growth rates.
Beige Book contacts do not represent a probability sample of U.S. households or firms.
No official source here establishes a causal impact on Korean exports, asset prices, or individual household outcomes.

rights_review.note: All source rights_status values remain unknown pending human review of page-specific terms. Article paraphrases facts and links originals; do not publish until rights review.

prohibited_claims: High-income households account for a quantified national share of spending.
September retail growth proves broad household purchasing power improved.
Beige Book is an official FOMC policy decision or a representative survey.
The figures predict Fed rate decisions, equity returns, or Korean exports.
recommended_structure: Open with the apparent gap between nominal sales and qualitative regional reports.
Explain measure, price adjustment, date, and coverage differences.
Analyze consumer-spending distribution without generalizing beyond source scope.
Contrast headline and core CPI and regional business cost reports.
Close with next data release and what remains unknown.
